name: Petrifying Well, Lymm
desc: A lime-laden spring by Ridding's Brook near Lymm Dam that turned mosses and twigs to stone, recorded by the Victorian botanist Leo Grindon; exact spot now uncertain, location approximate.

name: Billy Hobby's Well, Chester
desc: Spring on the edge of Chester known from 18th-century field names; 'Hobby' may echo the hob, a goblin or demon name, hinting at old folklore attached to the water.

name: Holy Well, Alderley Edge
desc: Spring beneath the Holy Well Rocks on Alderley Edge whose water was said in the 1840s to cure barrenness; a legend tells of a woman and cow buried by a falling boulder nearby.

name: St Ellen's Well, Harrisend Fell
desc: Lonely moorland holy well 500 ft up on Harrisend Fell above Scorton, marked on the 1846 map; today just a spring among reeds with no surviving stonework.

name: Holy Well, Didsbury
desc: Reputed ever-flowing spring near St James's old churchyard, once famed for health, magic and even prolonging life; believed lost to development.

name: Robin Hood's Well, Higham
desc: Icy spring above the River Calder below Pendle Hall, once valued as a cure for certain ailments; current condition unknown.

name: Holy Well, Hollinshead Hall
desc: Elegant stone well house built over a spring beside the ruins of Hollinshead Hall near Tockholes, where water pours from a carved lion's head; pilgrims once came for its reputed cure for eye complaints. Reached by woodland paths.

name: Fairy Well, Preesall
desc: Hilltop well at Preesall described in 1852 as all but deified; rags and clouts were tied to a nearby 'Beggar's Bush' with a prayer for healing.

name: Bull (Bel) Spring, Staining
desc: Spring issuing from a long stone mound at Hardhorn, linked by the Victorian cleric William Thornber to Hallowe'en bonfire cairns and seasonal rites; now largely forgotten.

name: Fairy Well (Wrangdomwell), Staining
desc: Cold spring between Hardhorn and Staining that local lore made a favourite haunt of kindly fairies, recorded by Rev. William Thornber in 1837.

name: Minspit Well, Preston
desc: One of Preston's earliest wells, at the foot of the Church Street ridge and long a healing and water source; destroyed by later development.

name: Calf Hey Well, Briercliffe
desc: Strong hillside spring rising into a square basin roofed with stone slabs; in medieval times its waters were believed to have special qualities.

name: Walloper Well, Newton-in-Bowland
desc: Roadside spring in Bowland where generations of travellers, drovers and lead miners stopped to drink; still flowing.

name: Dissenters' Well, Kelbrook
desc: Moorland spring near Kelbrook where Quakers, Baptists and other Nonconformists met for outdoor worship in the 17th-18th centuries, away from parish churches.

name: Peg o' Nell's Well (St Margaret's Well)
desc: Spring in the grounds of Waddow Hall by the Ribble, beside a headless statue probably of St Margaret; legend makes it the haunt of Peg o' Nell's spirit, whose statue was beheaded to lift her curse. Visible from the riverside footpath.

name: Our Lady's Well, Fernyhalgh
desc: Marian well beside a shrine chapel at Fernyhalgh, said to have been revealed to a storm-saved merchant in the 15th century; still a Catholic pilgrimage site.

name: St Helen's Well, Sefton
desc: Once a pyramid-roofed well house noted for icy water good for rheumatism and sprains; now capped with an inscribed stone, though parishioners still visit on the saint's day.

name: Shorey Well, Burnley
desc: Old Burnley well recorded by local antiquarian Clifford Byrne among the holy wells and healing springs of east Lancashire.

name: St Patrick's Well, Heysham
desc: One of two old holy wells in Heysham village; its water has been diverted and an iron pump in a stone arch now marks the spot.

name: Jinny Well, Newchurch-in-Pendle
desc: Spring trickling into a stone trough, haunted in folklore by Jinny's spirit, who wandered between the well and an old standing stone up the hill.

name: St Helen's Well, Colne
desc: Holy well at Waterside on the south side of Colne, relocated in recent years by local researchers after its memory survived in the name of the former St Helen's Mill.

name: St Helen's Wells, Whittle-le-Woods
desc: Celebrated well in a rugged part of Brindle parish where clear water bubbles through white sand; locals dropped crooked pins in for wishes, and its water was once carted round neighbouring villages for sale.

name: St Nicholas' Well, Carlisle
desc: Healing well near the medieval leper hospital of St Nicholas off Botchergate, prized for curing sores; people still filled 'shaking bottles' there in May in the 19th century. Destroyed by the railway.

name: St Cuthbert's Well, Carlisle
desc: Well in Carlisle's old market place linked to St Cuthbert's visit in 685 recorded by Bede; once sheltered by a pillared building called Carnaby's Folly, long since covered over.

name: St Helen's Well, Gosforth
desc: Spring at Newton near Gosforth named in a charter of c.1220 as St Helen's Well at the corner of a garden; possibly surviving as a boggy spring above the farm.

name: Holy Well, Humphrey Head
desc: Medicinal spring below the limestone cliffs of Humphrey Head, near caves called the Fairy Church and Fairy Chapel; lead miners stayed for days drinking its strange-tasting water to purge poisons.

name: St Cuthbert's Well (Helly-well), Waverbridge
desc: Once a copious spring of pure water where youths from surrounding villages held games on the second Sunday in May, with nothing stronger than the well water drunk; now only a trickle by a tree.

name: St John's Well, Dronfield
desc: Spring-fed well by Dronfield church, recorded c.1710 as the source of water for baptising infants; survives with an old stone-lined shaft in the courtyard of a 16th-century forge.

name: Nanny's Well, Chapel-en-le-Frith
desc: Chalybeate spring, perhaps named for St Anne, where locals made 'Spanish water' with sugar or liquorice on Easter morning; now a disused iron pump, still dressed and blessed each July.

name: Holy Well, King's Newton
desc: Holy well recorded from 1366, given an arched stone well house by the royalist Hardinge family in 1662; the collapsed arch was later rebuilt by the community.

name: St Alkmund's Well, Derby
desc: Well of the Saxon saint Alkmund, recorded from 1190, with steps down to an oval basin in an 18th-century niche; a vicar was reputedly cured by its water and it has been dressed at times. Now railed off in a housing area.

name: Hermit's Well, Dale Abbey
desc: Ever-flowing well beside the rock-cut hermitage at Dale Abbey, which the founding hermit is said to have dug and blessed as holy and a cure for all ills.

name: Silver Well, Ilkley Moor
desc: Never-failing spring by Silver Well cottage on Ilkley Moor, thought by Victorian writers to have been a holy well, perhaps once given silver offerings; now covered by stone slabs but still running.

name: Lady Well, Ackworth
desc: Ancient public well near Ladywell House in High Ackworth, probably dedicated to Our Lady; enclosed by the 1890s and now apparently lost, location approximate.

name: Wishing Well, Castley
desc: Spring beneath Chapel Hill above the Wharfe, under a hawthorn, where village girls once made wishes; tradition placed a small chapel above it. Now just a boggy patch in the trees.

name: Fairy Well, Nostell
desc: Well beside Fairy Wood near Nostell remembered in a local poem as a haunt of the little folk, who left when industry came; probable site only.

name: St Helen's Well, Barmby-on-the-Marsh
desc: Chalybeate well in St Helen's churchyard said to have medicinal powers; filled in during the 19th century and now remembered only in local memory.

name: St Peter's Well, Barmby-on-the-Marsh
desc: Sulphurous spring credited in 1831 with curing skin eruptions when applied externally; reportedly filled in during the 19th century and its exact position is now uncertain.

name: St Ann's Well, Welton
desc: Holy well that once supplied Welton House, possibly the source of the village name; it survives under stone slabs in a copse north of St Anne's College.

name: Fairy Well, Liversedge
desc: Ruined little well house beneath a sycamore, marked on the 1854 map; its fairy folklore is forgotten and water now seeps into a small bog nearby.

name: Old Wives' Well (Nattie Fontein), Stape
desc: Spring bubbling into a small stone-lined chamber on the moors near Pickering, its lintel crudely carved 'Nattie Fontein'; the 'Old Wife' name may recall an ancient earth goddess.

name: Holy Well, South Crosland
desc: Spring emerging from a blasted rock face into a round trough beside an older square cistern, remembered locally as a wishing well; often choked with litter.

name: St Peter's Well, Leeds (North Hall)
desc: Intensely cold spring near North Hall, long thought good for rheumatism and rickets and once served by a bathing house; covered over by 1846.

name: St Faith's Well, Leven
desc: Well by St Faith's Lane near the old churchyard, once the only drinking water for the Carrs; filled in c.1820 and its site re-found by a water diviner.

name: St Philip's Well, Keyingham
desc: Wishing well tied to the local saint Philip Inglebred, with a stone dated 1667; country girls dropped pins or sixpences in for luck. Now filled in, leaving only boggy ground.

name: St Hilda's Well (Seynt-Hild-keld), Whitby
desc: Spring near Grape Lane in Whitby recorded in 1396, later marked by the 'Virgin Pump' on Church Street; now destroyed, its site under a car park.

name: St Everilda's Well, Everingham
desc: Well of the 7th-century local saint Everilda in the grounds of Everingham Priory, once open to villagers and praised for abundant excellent water; filled in before 1923.

name: Low Well, Bradford
desc: Seemingly ordinary public well that local lore made Bradford's most supernatural water, haunted by ghosts and black dogs and used for scrying the future at 6 am.

name: Halliwell (Holy Well), Baildon
desc: Forgotten holy well below Halliway Banks Wood, recorded as Haliwell Bank in 1490 and reached by its own dedicated footpath on the 1852 map.

name: Cloven Hoof Well, Shipley Glen
desc: Free-flowing, drinkable spring in mossy Shipley Glen, mapped in 1852 as Raygate Well; a hoof-print mark on the rock below gives it its devilish name.

name: St Peter's Well, Leeds (St Peter's Square)
desc: Intensely cold sulphurous spring at the foot of High Street, used for cold bathing against rheumatism and rickets according to Ralph Thoresby in 1715; long built over.

name: Tun Well, Eccleshill
desc: Deep village well recorded from 1618 under a large slab on Tunwell Lane, a drought-time supply; folklore placed a phantom black dog and a white lady on the lane.

name: Brandy Well, Carlton Bank
desc: Roadside spring halfway up Carlton Bank whose peat-filtered water was said to have wonderful curative powers, with wishes made while drinking likely to come true; location approximate.

name: Mannerly (Manor Lea) Well, Gomersal
desc: One of Gomersal's main wells, where boys filled bottles with liquorice and treacle on Palm Sunday to make sweet 'Spanish water' and swap tastes.

name: Lady Well, Leeds
desc: Copious spring of soft water by Lady Lane near Quarry Hill, close to the medieval Chantry of Our Lady; now lost beneath city buildings.

name: St Francis' Well, Conisbrough
desc: Town well near the castle under a small steep-roofed conduit house; legend says a local holy man struck the spring from the ground during a drought in 1320-21. Now dry.

name: St Peter's Well, York Minster
desc: Ancient spring in the crypt of York Minster, traditionally where King Edwin was baptised at Easter 627, prompting the first wooden church on the site; no longer open to visitors.

name: Spink Well, Bradford
desc: Spring below which Spinkwell House offered health-giving cold baths from 1788; gravestones of 1645 plague victims were built into its well house. Now neglected and muddy.

name: Lady Well, Hartshead
desc: Clear spring flowing into a stone trough beneath an old hawthorn on Lady Well Lane leading to St Peter's Church; local tradition links it to baptisms by St Paulinus and to Robin Hood.

name: Birley Spa, Sheffield
desc: Spring developed as a cold bath in the early 1700s and rebuilt as a seven-bath spa by Earl Manvers in 1843; the restored bath house opens to the public on volunteer open days.

name: Crutch Well, Baildon
desc: Clear medicinal spring mapped in 1851, said never to run dry; it flows beneath the Cricketer's Arms opposite, keeping the cellar cool, with a cup-marked stone just above.

name: St Helen's Well, Eshton
desc: One of the most copious springs in England, boiling up into a circular pool by the road near Eshton Hall, recorded with a chapel in 1429; offerings are still tied to nearby shrubs. A listed monument.

name: Horncliffe Well, Hawksworth Moor
desc: Renowned moorland well recorded in 1273 at the meeting point of three townships, famed for never running dry even in 1976; sadly its flow has since failed.

name: New Edge Chalybeate, Colden
desc: Iron-rich spring trickling from an old stone trough beside New Edge above Colden, staining everything rust-red; such waters were valued for the blood and fatigue.

name: St George's Well, Harrogate
desc: Walled chalybeate spring off Parliament Street rediscovered c.1792, locally valued as an eye-wash for sore eyes before becoming one of Harrogate's spa wells; now lost.

name: St Sennen's Well, Sennen Cove
desc: Holy well 'of some repute' by the old Chapel Idne at Sennen Cove, whose water features in the Arthurian legend of the battle of Vellan-druchar; now lost, probably one of two mapped springs.

name: Holy Well, Lawhitton (Barton Farm)
desc: Holy well in a valley north of St Michael's church, recorded in 1914 and visited in 1980; by 1998 only a natural basin by a small bridge remained.

name: St George's Well (Fons George), Wilton
desc: Noted spring south of St George's church in Wilton, Taunton, where the afflicted came for cures said to be marvellous; its site was already uncertain by 1873, location approximate.

name: St Chad's Well, Logierait
desc: Renowned holy well behind Logierait church; tradition says its spirit was so offended when the saint's-day market on 22 August was stopped that the water vanished.

name: St Bride's Well, Port-na-Craig, Pitlochry
desc: Well by the medieval monks' ferry over the Tummel, dedicated to St Bride so travellers could seek her protection, usually by dropping in a brass pin or coin; lost about a century ago.

name: St Ninian's Well, Blairgowrie
desc: Well in Blairgowrie's Wellmeadow where tradition says St Ninian camped, drank and baptised converts; later covered over and piped into the town drains.

name: Whooping Cough Well (Sput na Fruith-chasd), Strathtay
desc: Spring spouting from a high rock by the Tullypowrie Burn, resorted to for curing whooping cough and counted among the three most important wells of the Tay valley; now overgrown.

name: Kinkhoast Well, Comrie
desc: Whooping-cough healing well in the hills above Comrie, recently revived and signposted by locals; its little pool is full of smooth white quartz pebbles left as offerings.

name: Lady's Well, Kincardine (Ardgay)
desc: Spring of excellent water at the foot of the 'Bank of the Gate' below the old Clan Ross castle site; the Ordnance Survey found it under the sea at high tide.

name: Holy Well, Glen Prosen
desc: Clear iron-bearing spring in remote Glen Prosen, reached by a straight stone-lined path from a ruined 17th-century chapel; a scatter of quartz stones may once have ringed it. Still drinkable.

name: Tobar Ruadh (Red Well), Heaste, Skye
desc: Roadside chalybeate well between Broadford and Heaste where travellers drank from a pewter mug; fishermen took its water to pregnant women in Elgol. Recently cleared, with a tin mug left at the roadside.

name: St Mary's Well, Inchberry
desc: Holy well and pool beside the Spey behind the Duff family mausoleum; pilgrims came on the first Sunday in May, leaving a stone offering, and its water was said to cure whooping cough, eye and joint troubles.

name: Holy Well by Loch ma Naire, Strathnaver
desc: Lost holy well near Loch ma Naire, where crowds came twice yearly before sunrise to bathe, walk round the loch, drink from the well and throw in coins for cures; location approximate.

name: St Helen's Well, Maybole
desc: Well on the old road to Ayr, famous in the 17th century for curing 'unthriving children', with crowds gathering especially at May Day; covered over in the 1950s.

name: Sulphur Well, Earlston
desc: One of Earlston's old 'verter' (virtue) wells, a sulphurous moorland spring whose 'gunpowder'-tasting water a local farmer credited with curing a serious internal complaint; lost in the 1800s, location approximate.

name: St Patrick's Well, Old Kilpatrick
desc: Well beside the church in the village that tradition claims as St Patrick's birthplace, used for baptisms and by villagers for centuries until closed in the 1890s; a later fountain nearby carried the name.

name: Holy Well, Tuxford
desc: Cold spring by Holywell Farm reputed to cure scurvy and other skin diseases and to help rheumatism, used for water until the 1920s; now a boggy patch.

name: Druid's Well, Sutton Park
desc: Spring beyond Bracebridge Pool in Sutton Park, once under a well house and much frequented in the 19th century; probably originally dedicated to St Mary. Now a stone-lined hole.

name: St John's Well, Berkhamsted
desc: Holy well, first linked to St James's chapel, where pagan-style rites drew a reprimand from Bishop Hugh of Lincoln in the 12th century; later a pilgrimage site whose water served a leper hospital.

name: St Cuthbert's Well, Bonnington (Leith)
desc: Chalybeate well by the Water of Leith, given a well house c.1818 where visitors paid a penny a drink; analysed as rich in iron salts, but destroyed in the 19th century.

name: St Stephen's Well, Banbury
desc: Slow chalybeate spring on the west side of Banbury, still often visited in 1841 and leaving a red deposit in its stone channel; built over later in the century.

name: Holy Well, Shoreditch
desc: The 'Haliwelle' recorded c.1100 that named Holywell Lane and the medieval priory, once sweet and frequented by scholars on summer evenings but spoiled by 1603; long destroyed.

name: St John's Well, Winkburn
desc: Holy well near Holywell Farm, probably linked to the Knights Hospitallers who held Winkburn manor; its water was said to be good for sore eyes. Now an overgrown muddy patch.

name: Bride's Well, Ballintemple
desc: Well beside a stream just north-west of an old church site in Co. Wicklow, probably dedicated to St Brigid; still visible in 1927 but now in woodland and condition unknown.

name: St Patrick's (Chapel) Well, Struthill
desc: Spring beside the overgrown ruins of a chapel by the Machany Water, so venerated that the Presbytery ordered the chapel demolished c.1650 to suppress the 'superstitions' practised there; now a boggy seep.

name: St Serf's Well, Ochtertyre
desc: Plentiful spring of St Serf, patron of Monzievaird, where on Lammas Day people drank and left white stones, spoons or rags; now drowned beneath the waters of the loch at Ochtertyre.

name: Mineral Wishing Well, Glen Lyon
desc: Gushing roadside mineral spring in Glen Lyon with a stone shelf for offerings, usually small pebbles, which were said to be replaced as fast as roadmen cleared them; offerings were still remembered in recent times.

name: Lady Well, Tibbermore
desc: Holy well of St Mary that gave Tibbermore ('great well') its name, near a church once held by the Bishops of Dunkeld; its site in a roadside paddock now shows no trace.

name: Chapel Well, Berryhill (Bankfoot)
desc: Holy well by a lost chapel and burial ground on the banks of the Ordie, where locals drank on the first Sunday of May until the 19th century; destroyed c.1850, site now in forestry.

name: St Patrick's Well, Dunruchan
desc: Boggy remnant of a holy well beside the lost chapel site just east of the Dunruchan standing stones; one of two St Patrick's wells in Muthill parish.

name: Holy Well of Inchadney (Beltane Well), Kenmore
desc: Quartz-edged well near a vanished church of the 'Holy Women', visited by crowds on Beltane morning until the mid-19th century; cleaning in 1914 turned up coins, buttons and a cross-marked stone.

name: Trinity Well, Trinity Gask
desc: Spring south of the manse famed in pre-Reformation times for miraculous cures and protection against plague and witchcraft; still flowing from a wooded bank in 2014.

name: St Mungo's Well, Gleneagles
desc: Strong cold spring gathering into a clear pool amid gorse in the Ochil foothills, mapped in 1860; no recorded traditions survive.

name: St David's (St Cuthbert's) Well, Weem
desc: Trickle collecting in a small stone pool beneath the crags of Weem Wood, once called St Cuthbert's Bath; later named for Sir David Menzies, who restored it and lived as a hermit in the nearby cave. Plaque and modern cross mark it.

name: St Mary's Well, Callander
desc: Quartz-lined holy well by the river at Callander, mapped in 1862 though overlooked by Scottish holy well surveys; still holding fresh water.

name: Maiden's Well, Glendevon
desc: Fine stone-bordered spring below fairy-haunted Maiden Castle, said never to fail; legend says a princess imprisoned in Castle Campbell was allowed out to drink here.

name: St Fillan's Well, Dundurn (Comrie)
desc: Healing spring said to have moved from the top of Dundurn hill to its foot in disgust; in 1791 seventy invalids came on 1 May and 1 August, walking sunwise three times, bathing, casting white stones on the saint's cairn and leaving rags. Especially sought by the childless.

name: St Bennet's Well, Cromarty
desc: Clootie well near the high-water mark below the ruined St Bennet's Chapel, where the sick drank and hung rags as offerings; in the 1930s wishers still left a scrap of clothing on the branches.

name: Holy Well of Isle Maree, Loch Maree
desc: Well of St Maelrubha on a sacred island in Loch Maree, famed for curing insanity; beside it stood a wishing tree so studded with hammered-in coins that it died. Reached only by boat.

name: St Francis' Well, Dundee
desc: Cold spring on the sunny slopes of the Greyfriars' meadows north of the Howff, dedicated by the friars and reckoned the favourite of Dundee's holy wells; repaired after the Reformation but long since lost.

name: Lady Well, Dundee
desc: Bright spring flowing from under the Chapelshade braes near the old Chapel of Our Lady, recorded in 1409 and later feeding the town's water supply; now drained beneath the Ladywell roundabout.

name: St Mary's Well, Lethnot
desc: Natural spring at the foot of a bank near Lethnot church, where silver coins left as votive offerings were found in the 19th century; the parish name may come from a word for a sacred place.

name: St Aidan's (St Iten's) Well, Menmuir
desc: Well by Menmuir church named for St Aidan of Lindisfarne, believed to cure asthma and skin diseases; drained in the 19th century, though water still issues from a roadside spout.

name: Holy Well, Balmossie Den
desc: Old wishing or holy well of Monifieth on the north side of the A92 at Balmossie Bridge, marked by a stone set up by Thomas Erskine in 1847 on the supposed medieval site, inscribed 'Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again'.

name: Lady Well, Airth
desc: Holy well below Airth Castle whose visitors were hauled before the kirk session in 1657 for leaving money, walking in silence and keeping the water from touching the ground; now destroyed.

name: St Ninian's Well, Stirling
desc: Ancient well in an old stone well house that gave its name to the St Ninians district of Stirling, beside a demolished chapel recorded from 1242.

name: St Maha's Well, Balmaha
desc: Healing spring high on the boggy moors above Balmaha, overlooking the islands of Loch Lomond; the village name is thought to come from the same saint.

name: Our Lady's Well, Stirling
desc: Holy well at the northern foot of Gowan Hill below Stirling Castle, drawn by J.S. Fleming in 1898; built over and destroyed in the 20th century.

name: Airthrey Mineral Wells, Bridge of Allan
desc: Cold mineral springs below the Ochils, noted by Defoe as useful against skin complaints, whose fame turned Bridge of Allan into a Victorian spa town; the old well house survives as a ruin.

name: Holy (Fairy) Well, Logie
desc: 'Very fine well' at the foot of Dumyat rising from over sixty springs through sand, described in 1792 as much resorted to by Catholics; still runs clear.

name: Chapel Well (Christ's Well), Cambusbarron
desc: Called the most famous of Stirling's holy wells, a village water supply and ritual site whose customs drew repeated church complaints; now marked only by a notice board.

name: Christ's Well, Blair Drummond
desc: Well where local people practised healing rites condemned in old church records, probably the 'Christ's Well' of Menteith described in 1618 as hung all about with rags; exact location disputed.

name: St Corbet's Well, Touch Glen
desc: Lonely spring in Touch Glen near Gilmour's Linn whose virtue lasted one hour a year: drinking at sunrise on the first Sunday of May was believed to preserve your life for twelve months. Long reduced to a boggy spring, location approximate.

name: St Finglassin's Well, Kinglassie
desc: Holy well of the saint who gave Kinglassie its name, sheltered by hawthorn and elder; the spring has been piped and bricked for water supply.

name: St Andrew's Well, Isle of May
desc: Walled spring beside the Altar Stones on the Isle of May, the island's best water and its main domestic supply, though prone to drying in summer.

name: Our Lady's Well, Gateside
desc: Small spring by the mill dam at Gateside beside the supposed site of St Mary's Chapel, remembered as a source of holy water before the Reformation.

name: Tobar Mor (Well of the Winds), Gigha
desc: Magical well on Cnoc Largie kept by an old woman guardian who, for silver, would clean it with a white clamshell, stir it sunwise and fling water toward the wind wanted by sailors; left uncovered it was said it could flood the island.

name: Tobar na h-Aoise (Well of Age), Iona
desc: Natural pool near the summit of Dun I on Iona, the 'well of eternal youth', where pilgrims came at dawn to touch the water as the first sunbeam struck it to renew their youth.

name: Tobar na Gaoithe Tuath (North Wind Well), Iona
desc: Lost magic well north of Cnoc nam Bradhan near the Hermit's Cell, where sailors left offerings to summon a north wind; location approximate.

name: Tobar nam Buadh (Well of Virtues), St Kilda
desc: Exceedingly cold spring near the Amazon's House on Hirta, described by Martin Martin in 1703 as a cure for colic, gravel and headaches; votaries once left humble offerings on a stone altar beside it.

name: Lighthouse Well, Dunnet Head
desc: The most northerly healing well on mainland Britain, a stone-surrounded spring with two troughs that also served the keepers of Dunnet Head lighthouse, who carried its water half a mile uphill.

name: Trows Well, Birsay
desc: Spring by the Loch of Boardhouse in Orkney once believed to be the home of a trow, the island troll; its folklore is now forgotten but the spring still flows.

name: Tobar na Cailleach, Keith
desc: Woodland 'well of the old woman' on Cairds Hill, once known for curing ailments and linked to a tale of the Cailleach bathing here and emerging young; still running as a dammed pool.

name: White Wells, Ilkley Moor
desc: Celebrated healing spring on Ilkley Moor, enclosed c.1760 by Squire Middleton in a white bath house with plunge baths for the 'cold water cure'; the building is open and water still runs into a plunge pool.

name: Holy Well, Hildenley
desc: Copious pure spring at the edge of Hildenley Wood near Malton running into a small well house and pool, said to have been much used by the monks of Kirkham Abbey and still credited with healing virtues in 1859.

name: St Helen's Well, Thorp Arch
desc: Ancient healing spring by St Helen's Beck in Chapel Wood near the Wharfe, close to a lost chapel and cross at St Helen's Ford; reputedly haunted and venerated since pre-Roman times.

name: St Helen's Well, Holbeck
desc: Medicinal holy well by St Helen's Bridge in Holbeck, once beside a chapel, later known as the Holbeck Spa Well; lost to industrial Leeds.

name: St Lambert's Well, Burneston
desc: St Lambert's 'fountain', recorded in the 12th century and probably in the present churchyard; it is thought to have given its name to the Halikeld ('holy spring') wapentake.

name: St Michael's Well, Well
desc: One of the springs that named the village of Well, where an iron cup once hung for travellers; a Roman bath house stood nearby.

name: Holy Well, Todmorden
desc: Spring of excellent water on the former Holy Well Lane, where local people once left 'memaws' — rags, coins and flowers — as offerings to the water.

name: Sore Eye Well, Eldwick
desc: Moorland well where people bathed their faces to cure poor sight and eye complaints, hanging rags on an old rowan tree as offerings; now under a water-authority cover.

name: Eyebright Well, Leeds
desc: Well near the Monk Pits recorded by Ralph Thoresby in 1715 as long esteemed a sovereign remedy for sore eyes; lost to the growth of Leeds in the 19th century.

name: Blind Well, Sutton-in-Holderness
desc: Healing well in the East Field near Spring Cottage Farm where villagers bathed sore eyes; long lost, location approximate.

name: Horley Green Spa, Halifax
desc: Chalybeate spring with May Day traditions, enclosed in a spa house and prominent in Calderdale's history from the late 18th to late 19th century.

name: Sulphur Well (Spa), Wigglesworth
desc: Sulphur spring under a small well house dated 1666, said in 1765 to have been used 'time out of mind' for healing.

name: Hawklemass Well, Whittingham
desc: Well with a stone trough near Howbalk Lane end, haunted by the 'Hawklemass Ghost', which village youths dreaded passing after dark.

name: Lee Hall Well, Bellingham
desc: 'Excellent spring' at Lee Hall where the lady of the hall dipped children with rickets on Whitsun, Midsummer and St Peter's Eves, said to bring either a speedy cure or death; exact spot lost, location approximate.

name: St Helen's (Freemen's) Well, Hartlepool
desc: Well in the Far-well Field beside the site of St Helen's Chapel, recorded c.1200; still visible in 1823 but now gone.

name: Bede's Well, Hebburn
desc: Well in a small railed amphitheatre, enclosed in 1932, which legend says Bede's monks visited from Jarrow for water; now dry after its spring was diverted by shipyard slag works.

name: Worm Well, Fatfield
desc: Wishing well at the foot of Worm Hill tied to the Lambton Worm legend, where crooked pins were offered and Midsummer Eve festivities held; reportedly restored in 1974.

name: St Martin's Well, Looe
desc: Spring flowing from a rock on the old parish boundary path above Looe, much used by villagers for its excellent water before being enclosed in a shed and piped to the town.

name: Holy Well, Gunwalloe
desc: Rock basin just below the porch of St Winwaloe's church on the shore at Gunwalloe, filled with sand at every high tide; already ruined by 1875.

name: St Agnes' Well, Cothelstone
desc: Scheduled well in a small well house, said to be a powerful wishing well for divining love, though some locals avoided it as a haunt of mischievous pixies.

name: Fairy Well, Barrow Gurney
desc: Spring in a dip by the stream near Barrow Wood, long visited to bathe sore eyes; a dedicated cup was kept there for drinking.

name: St Columb's Wells, Derry
desc: Three sacred springs outside Derry's walls named in the annals for Adomnán, Martin and Columba; already declining by 1837, now gone.

name: St Patrick's Well, Grianan of Aileach
desc: Well between the outer ramparts of the Grianan of Aileach where Patrick is said to have baptised Prince Eoghan; pilgrims once pushed pins into a tree beside it.

name: Our Lady's Well, Liberton
desc: Virgin Mary's well by the Braid Burn, praised in 1792 for its large flow and light, wholesome water; now lost.

name: Wells o' Wearie, Duddingston
desc: One of a ring of sacred and healing springs around Arthur's Seat, renowned for its water; disrupted when the railway cut into the hill, site approximate.

name: Druid's Well, Bingley
desc: Sweet spring seeping from beneath a lichen-covered boulder below the Druid's Altar crag near Bingley, near the lost 'Altar Well'.

name: Wallace's Well (Well of Spaw), Dunfermline
desc: Overgrown stone ruin of a reputed spring beside the path through Pittencrieff Glen, dedicated to William Wallace; in 1773 the council fought to keep the townsfolk's right of access to the 'Well of Spaw'.

name: Vicar's Well, Musselburgh
desc: Holy well by the Dam Brae, attached to the vicarage of St Michael's church and celebrated in 1857 for the excellence of its water.

name: Twentypenny Well, Duddingston
desc: Little-known healing well on the slopes of Arthur's Seat, still running clear into a stone trough by the path; its name may recall coin offerings.

name: St Michael's Well, Cowgate, Edinburgh
desc: Holy well of the dragon-slaying archangel near the Cowgate and St Mary's Street, shown on a sketch of the city c.1540; possibly remembered in the later 'Silverwell Close'. Long gone.

name: Old Wife's Spring, Snaizeholme
desc: Remote spring on a steep slope in Snaizeholme valley whose name may recall the Cailleach or old earth goddess; known only from place-name records.

name: Dragon's Well, Wharncliffe
desc: Well beneath Wharncliffe Crags where the legendary seven-headed Wharncliffe Dragon was said to drink, close to the Dragon's Den and the 'Old Wife's Cellar'.

name: Holy Ash Well (Hellywell), Bradford
desc: Healing spring of wide renown off Manningham Lane, with a Wart or Pin Stone beside it; now under or beside Valley Parade football ground.

name: Claymore Well, Kettleness
desc: Well near Kettleness where fairies were said to wash their linen and beat it with bittle and pin, the noise carrying a mile on fairy washing nights.

name: Craigie Well (Tobar Chragag), Avoch
desc: Black Isle rag well linked by some to the Virgin Mary, formerly visited on the first Sunday of summer; cloots were still being tied to nearby trees when recorded in 2014, though tree roots are toppling its stones.

name: St Plegmund's Well, Plemstall
desc: Medieval well dedicated to the Anglo-Saxon archbishop St Plegmund, possibly marking his hermitage; long known locally as a christening well. A scheduled monument, restored in 1907, though now without water.

name: St Oswald's Well, Winwick
desc: Stone-lined well chamber with steps down to the water, said to mark where King Oswald fell at the battle of Maserfelth; coins and objects were left here for healing. Scheduled monument, well kept by the community.

name: Chibbyr Undin (Well of the Ash), Grenaby
desc: Manx healing well near Grenaby: the sick drank, walked sunwise round it two or three times, then hung a wetted rag from their clothing on the hawthorn, expecting a cure as the cloth rotted.

name: St Maughold's Well
desc: Cliff-top spring above the sea by Maughold churchyard, said to be blessed by St Maughold; drinking while seated in the saint's rock chair was thought to help, especially women. Pilgrimage on the first Sunday in August; now a few tumbled stones.

name: St Winefride's Well, Holywell Farm, Clutton
desc: Large circular stone basin fed by several springs, one of a chain of wells said to mark the route of St Winefride's relics from Holywell to Shrewsbury; a medieval pilgrim station, its worn coping shows long use. Scheduled; in a private farm garden.

name: St Anne's Well, Sutton (St Helens)
desc: Medieval dressed-sandstone well basin by the brook dividing Rainhill and Sutton, reputed in the 19th century to cure eye complaints; its stone figure of a woman with a pitcher is long lost. Scheduled, partly silted.

name: Scarisbrick Park Holy Well
desc: Simple medieval roadside spring beside Southport Road, covered by an oval capstone carved with a small floriated cross and linked to the nearby wayside cross; a rare Lancashire survival. Scheduled.

name: Doon Holy Well, Kilmacrenan
desc: Pilgrimage well near Doon Rock, the O'Donnell inauguration site, said to have been blessed by a fasting priest; pilgrims make barefoot rounds and bathe limbs, and two rag trees hold medals, rosaries and other offerings. Well maintained and still busy.

name: St Declan's Well, Ardmore
desc: Clifftop wellhouse on St Declan's Way above Ardmore Bay, topped by worn crucifixion carvings; pilgrims make three rounds and drink the water, reputedly good for sore eyes, with a candlelit pattern on 24 July.
source: Holy Wells of Cork and Kerry

name: St Brigid's Well, Tully (Kildare)
desc: St Brigid's well near the ruined Black Abbey at Tully outside Kildare town, still a place of devotion; families traditionally came on her feast day, 1 February, to pray for health and fertility for household, stock and crops.

name: St Ciaran's Holy Well, Castlekeeran
desc: Group of rock-cut wells beside a great ash rag tree near Kells: one side of the healing well cures headaches, the other toothache, and a stone 'chair' eases back pain. Thousands attended its harvest-time pattern in the 1910s; three magical trout are said to appear.

name: St Ronan's Well, Marown
desc: Holy well in Marown parish in the island's central valley, recorded among the Manx sacred springs on the Megalithic Portal.

name: Glebe Well, Lonan Old Church
desc: Holy well by the ancient Lonan Old Church, listed among the island's sacred springs on the Megalithic Portal.

name: Chibbyr Roney
desc: Manx holy well recorded among the sacred springs of the Isle of Man on the Megalithic Portal; little tradition is recorded.

name: Chibbyr Pherick (St Patrick's Well), Peel Hill
desc: Well on the seaward side of Peel Hill below Corrin's Tower, said to have sprung where St Patrick's horse first touched land; drinking before sunrise on Old May Day with a wish was thought to make it come true, and silver was once left. Location approximate.

name: St Andrew's Well, Kirkandrews-on-Eden
desc: Medieval well in the churchyard at Kirkandrews-on-Eden, probably once used for baptisms.

name: St Cuthbert's Well, Edenhall
desc: Well by St Cuthbert's church at Edenhall, source of the legend of the 'Luck of Edenhall': fairies disturbed while drinking here are said to have left behind a medieval glass cup.

name: St Helen's Well, Great Asby
desc: Holy well at Great Asby in a stone enclosure probably of the 19th century; a Grade II listed structure.

name: St Michael's Well, Arthuret
desc: Well near St Michael's church at Arthuret, its structure probably dating from the 17th century.

name: St Ninian's Well, Brisco
desc: Ancient well with a 19th-century wellhead restored by Sarah Losh; well and wellhead are Grade II listed.

name: St Mungo's Well, Bromfield
desc: Medieval well near St Mungo's church, Bromfield, with a listed wellhead built in 1878.

name: St Patrick's Well, Patterdale
desc: Roadside holy well by Ullswater linked to St Patrick, sheltered by an 18th-century well house; the original spring may have been slightly elsewhere.

name: St Guron's Well, Bodmin
desc: Probably 15th-century granite well head beside St Petroc's church, Bodmin, its roof imitating slate courses; a carved panel shows St Guron, said to have founded a hermitage here in the 5th century, kneeling at the well. Grade II*.

name: St Ruan's Well, Grade-Ruan
desc: Small 15th-century granite well house on the Lizard, restored in the 19th century, keeping its corbelled roof, seat ledges and an empty niche; its gable cross is now in Grade church. Scheduled.

name: St Constantine's Well, Constantine Bay
desc: Holy well by a ruined chapel in the dunes, where pilgrims bathed their feet in water thought to have miraculous powers; lost to sand, re-excavated in 1911 and 1923, its basin still brims with clear water.

name: St Cyor's Well, Luxulyan
desc: 15th-century well house in a cobbled courtyard by Luxulyan church; dried up when a tramway cutting diverted its stream, but local people still leave fruit, flowers and candles inside. Scheduled.

name: St Neot's Well, St Neot
desc: Small medieval well house built into a bank with a granite slab roof and steps down to the water, inscribed as restored in 1852. Grade II.

name: St Urith's Well, Chittlehampton
desc: Well said to have sprung where the Anglo-Saxon virgin St Urith was beheaded with a scythe; sufferers of eye disease came to anoint themselves after St Peter's day, and pilgrim offerings helped build the church tower. Now a capped drystone well. Grade II.

name: St Bernard's Well, Edinburgh
desc: Mineral spring on the Water of Leith found c.1760 and compared to Harrogate water; in 1789 it was housed in a round Doric temple by Alexander Nasmith with a statue of Hygeia, restored in 1888.

name: Lady Well, Glasgow
desc: Artesian spring south of the Glasgow Necropolis in Dennistoun, older than the city itself, which stayed open as a public well after piped Loch Katrine water closed most others; reputedly Glasgow's last public well.

name: Leechwell, Totnes
desc: Triple spring in Totnes whose outlets are named Toad, Long Crippler and Snake, feeding three basins reached by three lanes; long used for healing, with a strong emphasis on the number three.

name: St Blaise's Well, Bromley
desc: Chalybeate spring in the grounds of the old Bishop's Palace at Bromley, reputed to heal and once a pilgrimage site with an oratory to St Blaise, patron of the wool trade.

name: Tanzie Well (St Anne's Well), Irvine
desc: Spring beside the River Irvine at the Golffields footbridge, also called St Anne's Well or the Spoot, perhaps a corruption of St Inan's Well; marked by a 1994 plaque.

name: Chapel Well (St Mary's Well), Irvine
desc: Shallow alcove well set into the wall of Chapel Lane by the River Irvine, with a plaque reading 'St Inan's Well AD839'; coins are thrown in for luck.

name: Kate's Well (St Catherine's), Shotts
desc: 15th-century spring well at the foot of Kirk o' Shotts church, where legend says the giant Bertram de Shotts was hamstrung and killed as he lay down to drink; restored in the 2000s.

name: Our Lady's Well, Hempsted
desc: 14th-century limestone well house built for Llanthony Priory's manor at Hempsted, carved on the back with St Anne, the Virgin and an angel; now dry. Grade I.

name: St Winifred's Well, Woolston
desc: Spring said to have gushed up where St Winifred's relics rested in 1138, famed among pilgrims for healing broken bones, with a second spring for eyes; red-spotted 'bloodstained' pebbles appear in it. Timber-framed well house above.

name: St Peter's Well, Houston
desc: Rare surviving holy well house over a spring below Greenhill Farm; its water was thought to protect travellers and ensure their safe return. Category B listed.

name: Maak's (Monk's) Well, Kilmaurs
desc: Possible holy well beside the Carmel Water below Kilmaurs Place, a public supply recorded in 1709 famed for never drying up; it stopped flowing in 2013.

name: Tobernalt Holy Well, Lough Gill
desc: 'Well of the cliff' near Lough Gill, an ancient spring said to have been a pagan gathering place and later a Penal-era Mass site, with a reputed healing stone nearby.

name: Dupath Well, Callington
desc: Almost intact late-medieval granite well house over a spring near Callington, dedicated to St Ethelred; its water was believed to cure whooping cough.

name: Elder Well, Blymhill
desc: Spring rising into a sandstone basin among elder trees at Blymhill Marsh, famed as a remedy for eye complaints; it was once dressed annually with flowers and branches amid rustic games.

name: Monk's Well, Wavertree
desc: Sandstone well on Mill Lane, Wavertree, dated 1414 and once topped by a cross, inscribed in Latin warning that the Devil laughs at anyone who gives nothing; alms supported the monks. Grade II.

name: St Aldhelm's Well, Doulting
desc: Never-failing spring at the source of the River Sheppey where St Aldhelm is said to have sat singing psalms on the day he died in 709; pilgrims bathed for healing, and flowers and offerings are still left.

name: Pipe Well (St Martin's Well), Liskeard
desc: Town well on Well Lane fed by four springs through lead spouts into a granite trough, recorded from the 14th century and said never to run dry; it had healing repute and a stone that brought luck in marriage to women who touched it.

name: St Cuan's Well, Ahascragh
desc: Walled holy well with a cross slab in Castlegar East near Ahascragh, protected as a National Monument; a pattern was held here on 15 October.

name: Lady's Well, Auchmannoch
desc: Spring by the Stra Burn ford near Auchmannoch House marked by a large inscribed red sandstone cross; remembered as a curative, wishing and clootie well where Mary Queen of Scots supposedly watered her horse.

name: St Fillan's Well, Kilallan
desc: Well beside the ruined church and rock 'seat' of St Fillan at Kilallan near Kilmacolm, site of the 7th-century cell of a saint so revered that his arm bone was carried before the Scots army at Bannockburn.

name: Menacuddle Holy Well, St Austell
desc: 15th-century well house in a wooded valley at St Austell, restored after the First World War by Admiral Graves-Sawle in memory of his son; drop in a pin and make a wish, and it will be granted.

name: St Queran's Well, Troqueer
desc: Spring-fed pool in a stone ring near Dumfries where coins and pins were left and ribbons tied to bushes in 1892; rags and offerings are still left today.

name: St Patrick's Well, Marlfield (Clonmel)
desc: Large bubbling basin beside a 12th-century church and an ancient cross west of Clonmel, visited by pilgrims for cures, especially of headaches; said never to freeze.

name: St Columbkille's Well, Inistioge
desc: Holy well reached by steps above Hatchery Lane, once the water source of the Augustinian priory, its well house built with salvaged priory carvings; the saint's day on 9 June was celebrated here.

name: St Cooey's Wells, Portaferry
desc: Three holy wells by a 7th-century church site on Tara Bay — one for washing hands, one for eyes, one for drinking — a major pilgrimage site from the 13th century, restored by the parish in the 1970s.

name: Struell Wells, Downpatrick
desc: Group of four holy wells with men's and women's bath houses east of Downpatrick, linked to St Patrick and still visited for cures; a chapel is recorded in 1306 and the buildings date from c.1600.

name: St Cuthbert's Well (Cuddy's Well), Bellingham
desc: Ancient holy well beside St Cuthbert's Church, Bellingham, which the saint is said to have found; a miraculous cure is told of a girl who drank from it. Water now runs through a Georgian 'pant' and is still used for baptisms.

name: St Ann's Well, St Anne's Park, Raheny
desc: Holy well under a stone hood in St Anne's Park, which takes its name from it; it dried up in the 1950s and remains dry, though the opening was cleared and grilled in 2018.

name: St Gobnait's Well, Ballyvourney
desc: Holy well on the site of St Gobnait's 6th-7th-century nunnery near Ballyvourney, with a circular path for praying the rounds and a 1951 statue of the saint by Séamus Murphy; still a popular pilgrimage site.

name: Sir John Schorne's Well, North Marston
desc: Village well blessed by the rector Sir John Schorne c.1290, which became a great pilgrimage resort after his death, its offerings paying to raise the church nave; renovated in 2004-05. Location approximate.

name: St Cubert's Holy Well (cave), Holywell Bay
desc: Holy well in a sea cave at Holywell Bay, emerging near a cleft in the rock through which children were passed to cure rickets. Tidal access; location approximate.

name: St Cleer's Holy Well
desc: 15th-century granite well house near St Cleer churchyard, built with a 'bowssening' pool for total immersion, with an old cross beside it.

name: St Clether Holy Well and Chapel
desc: Holy well and small chapel west of the church, among the best preserved in Cornwall, dedicated to St Clether, one of the children of the Welsh king Brychan.

name: Lady's Well, Woolpit
desc: Spring in a small tree-covered moated enclosure north-east of Woolpit church, named 'Our Ladys Well' in the 1570s and probably a medieval pilgrimage site linked to the church's shrine of the Virgin; a scheduled monument and nature reserve.

name: St Oswald's Well, Oswestry
desc: Spring said to have risen where a bird dropped the arm of the slain King Oswald, believed to cure eye trouble and possibly sacred before his time. Location approximate.

name: Tobar Chronain, Temple Cronan
desc: Holy well at the foot of a small cliff about 100 m south of the ruined oratory of Temple Cronan in the Burren, probably named after St Cronan. Location approximate.

name: St Maolrubha's Well, Ashaig, Skye
desc: Sacred spring said to have burst out when St Maolrubha tore a small tree from the ground, beside the rock he used as a pulpit; now under a stone well house, with a cross-marked stone found nearby.

name: Holy Well, Burton Dassett
desc: Holy well outside the church at Burton Dassett, in a stone well house, which still provides water.

name: St Mungo's Well, Caldbeck
desc: Holy well beside St Kentigern's church, Caldbeck, where Christians are said to have been baptised in the 6th century. Location approximate.

name: St Piran's Well, Trethevy
desc: Holy well beside the 15th-century St Piran's Chapel among farm buildings at Trethevy, covered by a mid-20th-century slate beehive topped with an iron cross.

name: St Morwenna's Well, Morwenstow
desc: Well halfway down the cliff west of Morwenstow church, said to have gushed out where St Morwenna rested while carrying a stone up for her church; now dry, in a Grade II well house.

name: Holy Well, Southam
desc: Mineral-spring well first recorded in 998, used by monks and long the town's main supply; water pours into the river through carved stone gargoyle mouths and was said to cure eye complaints. Restored 2005-07; scheduled.

name: Holy Well, Thornton-in-Craven
desc: Holy well of Saxon origin near St Mary's church, covered by an octagonal structure built by the rector in 1764; Grade II listed. Location approximate.

name: St Patrick's Well, Kiltubbrid
desc: Holy well beside the ruined church that gave Kiltubbrid ('church of the well') its name; folklore says it sprang up anew nearby after being filled in. Location approximate.

name: Holy Well (tree well), Kilkeasy
desc: Reputed holy well in Kilkeasy graveyard where the 'healing water', said to cure warts and sore eyes, collects in a hollow in a tree. Location approximate.

name: St Fachtna's Well, Tybroughney
desc: Holy well near the ruined parish church that gives Tybroughney (Tiobra Fhachna, 'Fachtna's well') its name; a pattern was held on 13 February, feast of the hermit St Modomnoc. Location approximate.

name: St Chad's Well, Chadwell
desc: Spring at the end of the mill pond in the hamlet of Chadwell, fed from a small clear pool across the road and described by Hope as approached by old stone steps.
